items.text: Maintain the child from the profits of the mother's lands, being its natural guardian.
items.quote: the husband is the natural guardian of the child, and as such is in reason entitled to the profits of the lands in order to maintain it

items.text: Provide for your children, since you have given them being.
items.citation: Blackstone, Commentaries, Book II, Chapter 14: Of Title by Descent · I
items.quote: as those to whom they have give being, and for whom they are therefore bound to provide

heading: Book II, Chapter 6: Of the Modern English Tenures · III.

items.text: Obtain the lord's permission before giving your daughter in marriage.
items.citation: Blackstone, Commentaries, Book II, Ch. 6, Of the Modern English Tenures, III.
items.quote: if the villein perfumed to marry his daughter to any one without leave from the lord
items.conflict: Treats children as property; parental authority is not subject to a feudal lord's consent (Gen 2:24).

items.text: Pay damages to the lord if you marry a villein's daughter without his leave.
items.citation: Blackstone, Commentaries, Book II, Ch. 6, Of the Modern English Tenures, III.
items.quote: the lord might also bring an action against the husband for damages in thus purloining his property
items.conflict: Marriage is a covenant between husband and wife before God, not a property transaction liable to a lord (Matt 19:6).

items.text: Account to the ward for the profits of the estate.
items.citation: Blackstone, Commentaries, Book II, Ch. 6, Of the Modern English Tenures, III.
items.quote: he, like guardian in socage, is accountable to his ward for the profits

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 6: Of the Modern English Tenures · II.

items.text: Account to him for the rents and profits of his land when he comes of age and demands it.
items.quote: call him to account for the rents and profits

items.text: Account to him for the value of the marriage if you gave him in marriage under fourteen, unless the marriage was to his advantage.
items.quote: he was bound to account to the ward for the value of the marriage, even though he took nothing for it, unless he married him to advantage

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 14: Of Title by Descent · II.

items.text: Admit him to the inheritance before any daughter.
items.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, Chapter 14: Of Title by Descent · II.
items.quote: sons shall be admitted before daughters

items.text: Though she is postponed to sons, admit her before any collateral relative.
items.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, Chapter 14: Of Title by Descent · II.
items.quote: daughters are excluded by sons, yet they succeed before any collateral relations

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 8: Of Freeholds, Not of Inheritance · IV.

items.text: Provide for your wife after your death by giving her dower in a third part of all lands you held in your lifetime.
items.quote: a widow shall be intitled for her dower to the third part of all such lands as the husband had held in his life time

items.text: Assign the widow her dower within forty days after her husband's death.
items.quote: The particular lands to be held in dower, must be assigned by the heir of the husband, or his guardian

items.text: If you are guardian of the heir, assign the widow her dower within forty days after her husband's death.
items.quote: The particular lands to be held in dower, must be assigned by the heir of the husband, or his guardian

items.text: Permit the widow to remain in her husband's capital mansion-house for forty days after his death while her dower is assigned.
items.quote: nothing shall remain in her husband's capital mansion-house for forty days after his death

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration

items.text: Leave to your wife her reasonable part of your goods; do not disinherit her.
items.quote: if he had no children, the wife was entitled to one moiety

items.text: Leave to your children their reasonable part of your goods; do not disinherit them.
items.quote: one went to his heirs or lineal descendants

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 8: Of Freeholds, Not of Inheritance · IV.

items.text: Restore the title deeds and evidences of the estate to the heir.
items.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, Chapter 8: Of Freeholds, Not of Inheritance · IV.
items.quote: detaining the title deeds, or evidences of the estate from the heir ; until she restores them

items.text: Do not alienate the land assigned for dower; if you do, you forfeit it to the heir.
items.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, Chapter 8: Of Freeholds, Not of Inheritance · IV.
items.quote: if a dowager alienes the land assigned her for dower, she forfeits it ipso facto, and the heir may recover it by action

items.text: If you make a jointure before marriage, ensure it takes effect immediately on your death, is for her own life, made to herself, and expressed as satisfaction of her whole dower.
items.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, Chapter 8: Of Freeholds, Not of Inheritance · IV.
items.quote: The jointure must take effect immediately on the death of the husband. It must be for her own life at least.

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration

items.text: Leave your wife her reasonable part of your goods, as the old common law reserved to her.
items.quote: this right of the wife and children was still held to be the universal or common law

items.text: Leave your children their reasonable part of your goods, as the old common law reserved to them.
items.quote: this right of the wife and children was still held to be the universal or common law

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration

items.text: As executor, pay the testator's debts before distributing legacies.
items.quote: his business first of all to see whether there is a sufficient fund left to pay the debts of the testator

items.text: If you have received a legacy, refund a ratable part if debts come in after legacies are paid.
items.quote: if the legatees have been paid their legacies, they are afterwards bound to refund a ratable part

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration

items.text: Pay his funeral charges and the expense of proving the will as the first debts.
items.quote: first, he may pay all funeral charges, and the expense of proving the will

items.text: Among simple contract debts, pay the servant's wages before any other.
items.quote: servants wages are by some with reason preferred to any other

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 8: Of Freeholds, Not of Inheritance · Notes

items.text: Be faithful to him; do not commit adultery.
items.quote: an adulteress was punished by the loss of her dotalitii et trientis ex bonis mobilibus viri

items.text: If you would keep your dower, remain chaste and do not remarry.
items.quote: dotem quidem babebit, dum corpus summ legitime servaverit — she shall have dower as long as she keeps her body lawfully
items.conflict: 1 Corinthians 7:39 permits a widow to remarry

items.text: Endow your wife at marriage with a dower or jointure to provide for her after your death.
items.quote: when he endowed her with personalty only, he used to say, “with all my worldly goods I thee endow;” which intitled the wife to her thirds

items.text: Provide a dowry for your wife at marriage.
items.quote: Dotem non uxor marito, sed uxori maritus assert — The husband gives a dowry to the wife, not the wife to the husband

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration · Notes

items.text: Ensure your widow receives her reasonable share of your goods: half if no children, a third if there are children.
items.citation: Commentaries, Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration · Notes
items.quote: uxores debent et solent habere suam rationabilem partem bonorum maritorum suorum — wives ought and are accustomed to have their reasonable part of their husbands' goods

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration

items.text: Administer his estate faithfully: pay his lawful debts and render an account as an executor would.
items.quote: administrators are put upon the same footing, with regard to suits and to accounting, as executors appointed by will.

items.text: Give her the portion due to her by law (pars rationabilis) from the estate.
items.quote: the partes rationabiles, or two thirds, of the wife and children were deducted

items.text: Give them the portions due to them by law (partes rationabiles) from the estate.
items.quote: the partes rationabiles, or two thirds, of the wife and children were deducted

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration

items.text: Do not disinherit or pass over any of your children without a true and sufficient reason; leave them at least a small legacy.
items.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, II.32, Of Title by Testament, and Administration
items.quote: deficient in natural duty, if they disinherited or totally passed by (without assigning a true and sufficient reason) any of the children

items.text: After you marry and have a child, revoke or alter a will made in celibacy so that your child is not left unprovided.
items.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, II.32, Of Title by Testament, and Administration
items.quote: if a man, who hath made his will, afterwards marries and hath a child, this is a presumptive or implied revocation of his former will

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration

items.text: If your father advanced you during his lifetime, bring that sum into account with your brothers and sisters before taking any further share under the custom.
items.quote: if any of the children are advanced by the father in his lifetime with any sum of money (not amounting to their full proportionable part) they shall bring that portion into hotchpot with the rest of the brothers and sisters, but not with the widow, before they are intitled to any benefit under the custom

items.text: As administrator of the estate, set aside for the widow her customary portion: one-third if there are children, one-half if not, besides her apparel and bed-chamber furniture.
items.quote: If the deceased leaves a widow and children, his substance (deducting the widow's apparel and furniture of her bed-chamber...) is divided into three parts; one of which belongs to the widow, another to the children, and the third to the administrator: if only a widow, or only children, they shall respectively, in either case, take one moiety, and the administrator the other

items.text: As administrator of the estate, give to the children their customary portion: one-third if a widow survives, one-half if not.
items.quote: one of which belongs to the widow, another to the children, and the third to the administrator: if only a widow, or only children, they shall respectively, in either case, take one moiety, and the administrator the other

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration

items.text: Do not bequeath your personal chattels without your husband's licence, for they are his by law.
items.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, Chapter 32
items.quote: she is incapable of making a testament of chattels, without the licence of her husband. For all her personal chattels are absolutely his own

items.text: If you covenanted to allow her to make a will, honor that covenant and allow her appointment to stand.
items.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, Chapter 32
items.quote: the husband by his bond, agreement, or covenant, is bound to allow

items.text: Do not claim or control goods she holds as executrix or administratrix; those never become your property.
items.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, Chapter 32
items.quote: any feme-covert may make her will of goods, which are in her possession in auter droit, as executrix or administratrix; for these can never be the property of the husband

items.text: Allow her to dispose of her pin-money or separate maintenance savings by will without your control.
items.citation: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, Chapter 32
items.quote: if she has any pinmoney or separate maintenance, it is said the may dispose of her savings thereout by testament, without the control of her husband

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 8: Of Freeholds, Not of Inheritance · IV.

items.text: Remain faithful: do not elope or live with an adulterer.
items.quote: if a woman elopes from her husband, and lives with an adulterer, she shall lose her dower

items.text: Give her the dower: one third of the lands for her life.
items.quote: the wife shall have the third part of all the lands and tenements whereof he was seised during the coverture
items.needs_role: heir (the person who inherits the husband's lands)

items.text: Provide for her sustenance.
items.quote: for the sustenance of the wife

items.text: Provide for the nurture and education of your younger children.
items.quote: and the nurture and education of the younger children

work: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book II, chapters 6, 8, 14, 32
heading: Book II, Chapter 32: Of Title by Testament, and Administration

items.text: Give the widow one third of the intestate's personal estate, or one half if there are no children or their representatives.
items.quote: One third shall go to the widow of the intestate

items.text: Divide the residue equally among the children, or to their lineal descendants if any child is dead.
items.quote: the residue in equal proportions to his children, or, if dead, to their representatives; that is, their lineal descendants

items.text: If there is no widow or children, distribute the whole estate among the next of kin in equal degree and their representatives.
items.quote: if neither widow nor children, the whole shall be distributed among the next of kin in equal degree, and their representatives

items.text: Share the inheritance equally with brothers and sisters, counting any lifetime advancement from the parent toward your portion.
items.quote: the children so advanced shall now have so much as will make them equal
